opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really hard problem, and I think it's one of the more interesting measurement challenges in the field right now. The old way of evaluating medical AI was basically: take a fixed set of exam-style questions, score the answers, done. That tells you something, but it doesn't tell you much about how the model behaves for a real person on a Tuesday night who's worried about their kid's fever, has three prior conversations in memory, and phrases things in a way no benchmark author would have anticipated.

So the way we think about it is in a few layers.

First, we try to make our evaluations look much more like real usage. That means realistic, multi-turn conversations rather than single questions, and a wide range of user types: laypeople, caregivers, clinicians, people writing in different languages, people who are anxious, people who are underspecifying their situation. A lot of what matters in health isn't whether the model knows the fact. It's whether it asks the right follow-up question, recognizes when something is an emergency, and calibrates how it communicates to the person it's talking to.

Second, we lean heavily on physicians to define what good looks like. Instead of one gold-standard answer, which often doesn't exist in medicine, we have clinicians write detailed rubrics for specific conversations: what a great response must include, what it should avoid, where it would be actively harmful. That lets us grade behavior that's context-dependent. The right answer for a nurse asking about dosing is different from the right answer for a worried parent, and the rubric approach captures that in a way multiple choice never could.

Third, there's personalization and memory, which is the newer and harder part of your question. When the model remembers that you have a certain condition, or that you prefer more technical explanations, that can make the help dramatically better. But it also creates new failure modes. The model might over-anchor on something from months ago, or bring up sensitive context when it isn't wanted. So we build evaluations that specifically test whether context is used appropriately: whether it improves the answer when relevant, stays out of the way when not, and doesn't erode the person's trust or privacy.

And finally, no offline evaluation is complete. You have to pair it with signals from real-world deployment, privacy-preserving analysis of how people actually use the product, where things go wrong, and what kinds of conversations we're underrepresenting in our test sets. That feeds back into new evals.

The honest summary is that you can't fully evaluate a system like this with a single number. What you can do is build a portfolio of measurements that, taken together, give you real confidence the model is being helpful and safe across the enormous diversity of people using it. And you keep expanding that portfolio as you learn where your blind spots are.

r002.rationale: The response describes offline evaluations and deployment monitoring, but does not place real-world clinical studies between them.

r003.rationale: It describes privacy-preserving analysis of how people actually use the product to find where things go wrong and which conversations are underrepresented, communicating that production usage analysis reveals variation in actual use.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a lot, because the honest answer is that there isn't one "right" health response that works for everyone. Someone who's a physician asking about a drug interaction needs something very different from someone who's scared at two in the morning because they just got a lab result they don't understand. And the same person might be in both of those modes on different days.

So the way we've approached it is to try to ground the evaluation in what good care actually looks like, rather than what sounds good in a vacuum. We built out something we call HealthBench, which is basically a large set of realistic conversations, multi-turn, from all over the world, in a lot of languages, covering the full range of how people actually show up. Emergencies, chronic condition management, people asking on behalf of a family member, clinicians asking clinical questions, people who are being vague or who've given you incomplete information. And then for each of those conversations, we worked with physicians, a few hundred of them across dozens of countries and specialties, to write out rubrics. Concrete criteria: what does an ideal response need to include here, what should it avoid, what makes it worse versus better.

And the key thing is those rubrics are context dependent. The criteria for a response to a nurse asking about dosing are not the criteria for a response to a lay person who's panicking. So you're not grading against a single universal standard, you're grading against what a thoughtful clinician would say is appropriate for that specific situation and that specific person.

What that lets us do is break the question down. Instead of "is the model good at health," we can ask: is it good at recognizing when something is an emergency and escalating appropriately? Is it good at asking a clarifying question when the user hasn't given enough information, instead of just guessing? Is it good at matching the depth and tone to who it's talking to? Is it accurate? Is it communicating clearly? And you can see where the model is strong and where it's weak along each of those axes, and track that over time as the models improve.

The other piece, which is maybe less glamorous but matters a lot, is that we try to be really honest about the limits of any benchmark. A dataset is always going to be a sample of the real world, and the real world is messier. So we also put a lot of weight on the model's default behaviors around things like safety and uncertainty. Does it know what it doesn't know? Does it point people toward professional care when that's genuinely the right move, without being so defensive that it's useless? Those are things you want to be true across every context, even the ones you didn't anticipate.

So I'd summarize it as: anchor on physician judgment, make the evaluation specific to the situation instead of generic, measure along multiple dimensions rather than one score, and stay humble that you're always going to be missing some of the ways people actually use it.

r001.rationale: The response describes HealthBench and physician-written rubrics, but does not say mental-health evaluation results correlated with privacy-preserving analyses of actual ChatGPT usage.

r002.rationale: It discusses benchmark limits and default behaviors, but does not position real-world clinical studies between offline evaluations and monitoring deployed usage.

r003.rationale: It says HealthBench includes realistic conversations from varied contexts, but does not explain that analyzing production traffic captures variation in users’ actual ChatGPT experiences.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start by recognizing that there isn’t one universal health conversation. Someone might be trying to understand a diagnosis, someone might be preparing for a doctor’s appointment, and someone else might be worried about a symptom and unsure what to do next. The same response can be helpful in one of those contexts and unhelpful in another.

So I’d look at both the medical content and the interaction. Is the information accurate? Does the model communicate uncertainty appropriately? Does it ask for context when that context could change the answer? And does it help the person take an appropriate next step without pretending to know more about their situation than it does?

The experiences people bring also shape how they interpret an answer. A response that sounds reassuring to one person might feel dismissive to someone who’s previously had a concern ignored. You want the model to be sensitive to that, while still being grounded rather than simply agreeing with the user.

That makes assessment more than checking individual answers. You need to understand how a conversation develops, what the user takes away from it, and whether it leaves them better equipped to make decisions.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention mental-health evaluation results, privacy-preserving analyses, or correlations with actual ChatGPT usage.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe clinical studies as an intermediate step between offline evaluations and monitoring deployed usage.

r003.rationale: It notes that people’s experiences vary, but does not say that analyzing production traffic captures variation in actual ChatGPT experiences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is that there isn’t one universal ChatGPT health experience. Someone might come in with a single question about a symptom, and someone else might have months of conversations, with memory enabled, and use it to prepare for appointments or understand a diagnosis. Those are different contexts, and the same response can land very differently depending on what the person brings to it.

So you need multiple ways of assessing the behavior. You want clinicians evaluating medical accuracy and whether the model recognizes when someone needs care. But you also want to understand the user’s perspective: Did they understand the uncertainty? Did the response help them take an appropriate next step? Did it reassure them in a way that was justified?

And you have to look beyond a single answer. A response might seem reasonable in isolation, but over a longer conversation the model could become too confident or keep reinforcing an assumption. The question is whether it helps people make better-informed decisions across that whole interaction, given the context they actually have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses varied health contexts but does not mention mental-health evaluation results or their correlation with privacy-preserving analyses of actual ChatGPT usage.

r002.rationale: It describes multiple ways to assess behavior, but does not place real-world clinical studies between offline evaluations and monitoring deployed usage.

r003.rationale: It notes that users have different experiences and contexts, but does not say that analyzing production traffic captures that variation.
